items.title: Weighted categorical choice
items.mechanism: Choose one discrete outcome using nonnegative weights normalized to a probability distribution.
items.mapping: Use candidate motifs, chord functions or articulations as outcomes. Filter illegal candidates before normalization, so randomness selects a musically meaningful alternative.
items.example: For tonic, predominant and dominant weights [5,2,3], probabilities are [.5,.2,.3]. This does not require the next ten choices to contain exactly five tonics.
items.controls: Energy can favour active variants; emotion changes profile-specific weights; section time can increase a cadence weight.
items.failure: Independent choices forget context. All-zero weights need an explicit fallback; peaked weights can trap the piece.
items.experiment: Compare empirical frequencies over many seeds, then listen for direction with and without phrase constraints.

items.title: Bernoulli gates and stochastic masks
items.mechanism: Each eligible slot has a binary success probability.
items.mapping: Apply gates to optional attacks while preserving motif anchors. Keep the mask keyed by bar, part and slot so overlapping queries agree.
items.example: An eight-slot pattern with p=.25 has two expected retained attacks, but a particular bar can contain none. Reserve the first anchor separately.
items.controls: Energy controls eligible-attack probability; emotion may favour particular metric positions without changing total expectation.
items.failure: Expectation is not a hard density limit. Independent gates can erase the theme or create unbalanced clusters.
items.experiment: Check anchor survival and aggregate caps; compare independent gates with exact-count selection at matched mean density.

items.title: Poisson counts and event clouds
items.mechanism: A Poisson variable models counts with a specified mean; an ideal homogeneous Poisson process has exponentially distributed waiting times.
items.mapping: Choose the number of ornamental events in a musical window, then map positions and pitches through the current profile.
items.example: At mean three attacks per bar, zero attacks has probability exp(-3), about .0498. Capping the count at six changes the resulting distribution.
items.controls: Energy steers the mean; section envelopes steer its trajectory; emotion selects register and articulation independently.
items.failure: Unrestricted clouds can cluster or overwhelm other parts. Quantizing or adding minimum spacing changes the ideal process.
items.experiment: Measure uncapped and capped count distributions separately and inspect silence, clustering and foreground clarity.

items.title: Renewal processes for rhythm
items.mechanism: Generate successive inter-event intervals from an interval distribution.
items.mapping: Use a rhythmic alphabet such as half, one and two beats instead of assuming every event occupies the same grid slot.
items.example: Intervals [1,.5,.5,2] sum to a four-beat bar. A newly drawn interval that exceeds the phrase needs a declared trim, defer or rejection policy.
items.controls: Energy changes interval weights; emotion can alter long-short contrast; time supplies phrase boundaries.
items.failure: Independent intervals can drift across bars. A final forced interval can create a conspicuous repair.
items.experiment: Compare unconstrained renewal, conditional bar filling and authored rhythmic cells under identical budgets.

items.title: Bounded random walks
items.mechanism: Update a state by sampled increments, with explicit boundary handling.
items.mapping: Walk through scale degrees or voicing indices. Reflection keeps motion in a tessitura while preserving a sense of local movement.
items.example: In degrees 0..6, a proposed step from 6 to 7 reflects to 5 under a reflecting policy; clamping instead stays at 6.
items.controls: Energy may expand the step distribution; emotion can bias direction; a phrase target can constrain the final steps.
items.failure: Clamping accumulates visits at boundaries; wrapping creates leaps; unconstrained walks meander without endings.
items.experiment: Compare boundary occupation, leap distributions and cadence arrival for reflecting, clamped and wrapped versions.

items.title: Mean-reverting stochastic control
items.mechanism: Combine random perturbation with attraction toward a reference value.
items.mapping: Drive register centre, gate ratio or ornament preference toward a profile target while allowing temporary excursions.
items.example: Use x_next=x+theta*(mu-x)*dt+sigma*sqrt(dt)*z, then map x to a bounded control. This is a numerical proposal, not an exact continuous-time simulator.
items.controls: The emotion selects mu; energy selects a bounded fluctuation range; time determines dt and target transitions.
items.failure: Large integration steps can destabilize the process. Rounding continuously to a pitch can create repetitive threshold chatter.
items.experiment: Check time-step sensitivity, recovery after perturbation and whether continuous variation survives musical quantization.

items.title: Coloured-noise control trajectories
items.mechanism: Correlate random values across time through filtering or a prescribed spectral construction.
items.mapping: Use slow correlated fluctuations for density or register instead of unrelated per-note random values. The output remains a symbolic control curve.
items.example: Smooth [0,1,0,1] before mapping to an ornament chance; hold the resulting value for a bar rather than jittering each attack.
items.controls: Energy sets range, emotion sets baseline and correlation time; keep the sampling interval fixed or accounted for.
items.failure: A generic low-pass filter is not automatically exact pink noise. Spectral slope does not establish musical coherence.
items.experiment: Compare independent, smoothed and explicitly specified pink-noise controls using the same mean and variance.

items.title: Correlated multivariate sampling
items.mechanism: Sample related variables jointly rather than choosing every dimension independently.
items.mapping: Couple gate, accent and leap preferences through a valid covariance structure, then project into allowable musical ranges.
items.example: A profile might correlate larger leaps with longer gates but keep attack count independent, producing room for a leap to register.
items.controls: Energy can alter variance; emotion selects a tested coupling profile; change covariance at phrase boundaries.
items.failure: A non-positive-semidefinite covariance is invalid. Clipping and quantization can substantially change the intended correlations.
items.experiment: Inspect realized score correlations and compare them with the latent sampled values, not just the requested matrix.

items.title: Low-discrepancy and quasi-random exploration
items.mechanism: Generate deterministic points that cover a parameter space more evenly than ordinary independent sampling in a specified sense.
items.mapping: Explore combinations of motif transformation, register and density when building an audition library.
items.example: Use a two-dimensional Sobol design to audition register spread and gate ratio, then compare coverage with the same number of random proposals.
items.controls: Emotion selects a region of the library; energy selects its density coordinate; time orders the selected transitions musically.
items.failure: Coverage is not musical variety. Sobol balance properties require attention to sample counts and sampling method.
items.experiment: Measure parameter coverage and duplicate realized scores; listen after arranging candidates into phrases.

items.title: Bayesian preference updating
items.mechanism: Update a prior belief with explicit observations, retaining uncertainty.
items.mapping: Learn session-local acceptance rates for optional motifs or actions from deliberate feedback, not from every Stop gesture.
items.example: A Beta(1,1) prior plus three accepts and one reject becomes Beta(4,2), with mean 2/3. Feedback quality still determines meaning.
items.controls: Keep separate contexts for profile, emotion and energy; use session time for optional forgetting rather than treating old judgments as permanent.
items.failure: Acceptance can reflect timing or usability rather than musical taste. Sparse contexts can encourage overconfident personalization.
items.experiment: Compare calibrated predictive uncertainty and useful recommendations against a fixed-preference baseline.

items.title: First-order Markov chains
items.mechanism: The next-state distribution depends on the present state.
items.mapping: Represent states as scale degrees, rhythmic cells or harmonic functions. Add metric and cadence constraints outside the chain.
items.example: For C,D,E states, C may transition to D with .75 and E with .25. Sampling follows that row; it does not understand a phrase ending.
items.controls: Blend valid transition matrices at phrase boundaries; energy controls rhythmic emissions, while emotion chooses profile-conditioned alternatives.
items.failure: Dead rows, absorbing states and short loops need explicit handling. A chain can imitate local habits while losing long-term form.
items.experiment: Check row sums and empirical transitions, then compare phrase closure and theme recall with a conductor added.

items.title: Higher-order Markov and n-gram models
items.mechanism: Condition the next event on a fixed-length history of previous symbols.
items.mapping: Use recent intervals and duration categories to preserve recognizable cells beyond one step.
items.example: Histories [0,2] and [4,2] can lead to different continuations although their last degree is the same. An unseen pair needs backoff.
items.controls: Emotion changes candidate preferences after prediction; energy changes rhythm conditioning; phrase time adds target information.
items.failure: The number of contexts grows rapidly and sparse training can copy fragments or leave dead ends.
items.experiment: Compare several orders with held-out sequences and track repeated training fragments separately from likelihood.

items.title: Variable-order Markov and prediction by partial matching
items.mechanism: Use longer contexts when supported and shorter ones when data are sparse.
items.mapping: Model intervals, rhythm and metrical viewpoints with explicit smoothing, borrowing the predictive framing of IDyOM.
items.example: If a three-event history is unseen, consult its two-event suffix and shorter contexts; specify interpolation rather than inventing probability mass.
items.controls: Energy can steer rhythmic candidates after prediction; emotion can choose a corpus/profile; freeze context at the composition boundary.
items.failure: Backoff design affects surprise estimates. A predictive model is not automatically a generative aesthetic policy.
items.experiment: Evaluate held-out prediction and generated phrase structure separately; record which context lengths contributed.

items.title: Hidden Markov models
items.mechanism: A latent Markov state governs the distribution of observed events.
items.mapping: Let hidden states represent phrase roles such as statement, response and closing, with separate note/rhythm emissions.
items.example: A closing state can favour long tonic-related events while an active state favours short connecting notes. States need not equal emotion labels.
items.controls: Emotion biases allowable emissions; energy adjusts activity within a state; time and minimum residence prevent flicker.
items.failure: Learned states may not match named musical roles. Ordinary HMM duration behaviour may produce implausibly rapid state changes.
items.experiment: Inspect state occupancy and emitted music; compare with an explicitly authored role-state controller.

items.title: Semi-Markov and explicit-duration models
items.mechanism: Model state residence durations explicitly instead of letting transitions alone determine them.
items.mapping: Represent section or phrase roles whose lengths matter musically, while a lower-level generator fills their material.
items.example: Choose a contrast duration from four or eight bars, then generate its phrase events without resampling its role every beat.
items.controls: Energy can influence allowed duration weights; emotion affects texture; ending requests override only at valid boundaries.
items.failure: Too many duration options dilute form. Truncating a sampled duration can invalidate the model assumptions.
items.experiment: Compare residence-length distributions and audible section clarity against a memoryless state-transition baseline.

items.title: Factorial and factored state models
items.mechanism: Represent several interacting latent or observed state components rather than one undifferentiated state label.
items.mapping: Separate harmonic region, texture and rhythmic activity, then constrain incompatible joint combinations.
items.example: A stable harmony can coexist with an active texture; changing the texture state need not reset the harmonic route.
items.controls: Emotion steers selected factors; energy steers activity; section time arbitrates simultaneous transitions.
items.failure: Independent factors can create musically incompatible combinations. The full joint state space can still grow combinatorially.
items.experiment: Compare factor independence with constrained coupling and count rejected joint states alongside listening judgments.

items.title: Constrained Markov generation and endpoint bridges
items.mechanism: Condition sequence sampling on admissibility rules or a required future endpoint.
items.mapping: Choose a cadence target first, then favour transitions that can still reach it in the remaining slots.
items.example: If only two events remain and a target is unreachable from one candidate, reject it or compute endpoint-conditioned transition weights.
items.controls: Emotion changes the valid route vocabulary; energy changes optional subdivisions; time supplies the remaining horizon.
items.failure: Simply forcing the last note can create an awkward leap. Filtering transitions requires renormalization and dead-end detection.
items.experiment: Check endpoint reachability and compare whole-route conditioning against last-note replacement.

items.title: Time-inhomogeneous Markov chains
items.mechanism: Allow the transition matrix to vary with a declared time or control variable.
items.mapping: Move from stable to exploratory harmonic preferences across a section without replacing the state vocabulary.
items.example: If matrices A and B are row-stochastic, (1-w)A+wB remains row-stochastic for 0<=w<=1. That does not preserve every stationary property.
items.controls: Use smoothed wheel intensity for w; keep energy in rhythm decisions; commit matrix changes at an explicit boundary.
items.failure: Fast changes can erase learned local habits. Interpolating matrices is not proof of perceptually linear emotion change.
items.experiment: Verify nonnegative normalized rows and compare the requested blend with actual realized harmonic behaviour.

items.title: Factor-oracle recombination
items.mechanism: Use a compact sequence automaton and shared-context links to recombine observed material.
items.mapping: Store interval/rhythm tuples from authored or session motifs and jump between context-compatible continuations.
items.example: Two motifs sharing the suffix [up-step,repeat] can offer different next cells; filter the proposed continuation against the current harmony.
items.controls: Energy selects rhythmic variants; emotion biases eligible continuations; phrase time controls jump opportunities.
items.failure: Context-compatible symbols can still make poor phrase joins. Recombination can overuse a small source corpus.
items.experiment: Track jump points, source provenance and listener-recognized continuity; compare with simple cell concatenation.

items.title: Reinforced sampling and Polya-urn memory
items.mechanism: Increase an outcome weight when it is selected, creating history-dependent reinforcement.
items.mapping: Give a motif recurring presence within one session, while a decay or cap keeps one idea from taking over.
items.example: Starting weights [1,1], selecting A and adding one gives [2,1], so the next probability of A is 2/3.
items.controls: Emotion can choose eligible motif families; energy affects realization, not reinforcement; time can decay old weights.
items.failure: Unbounded reinforcement can lock into an arbitrary early choice. Frequency is not a measure of quality.
items.experiment: Compare reinforced, decayed and unreinforced recall under matched seeds and explicit motif-retention goals.

items.title: Genetic algorithms for phrases
items.mechanism: Evolve a population using selection, recombination and mutation over an explicit representation.
items.mapping: Encode a phrase as rhythmic cells, degree anchors and articulation genes. Decode and validate before calculating musical criteria.
items.example: Cross two four-cell phrases only at cell boundaries, preserve their cadence anchor, then mutate one optional interval.
items.controls: Energy selects density objectives; emotion selects profile preferences; evolution prepares future phrases outside the commitment window.
items.failure: Fitness can reward bland repetition; naive crossover breaks meter and voice-leading. More generations do not prove better music.
items.experiment: Compare against equal-budget random search, log objective components and audition held-out seeds.

items.title: Typed genetic programming
items.mechanism: Evolve programs or expression trees rather than only fixed-length parameter vectors.
items.mapping: Use typed operators such as sequence, rotate, mask and transpose; terminals are motifs or bounded patterns.
items.example: A valid tree can be rotate(sequence(m1,m2),oneBeat). Forbid an operator whose expansion exceeds the phrase event budget.
items.controls: Emotion ranks transformations; energy bounds expansion; time selects when a generated program becomes active.
items.failure: Tree bloat and unrestricted evaluation threaten deadlines. Program validity does not ensure musical coherence.
items.experiment: Measure tree size, event expansion and motif preservation; compare learned trees with a small authored grammar.

items.title: Grammar-guided evolutionary encoding
items.mechanism: Decode an evolving genotype through a constrained production grammar.
items.mapping: Evolve phrase plans that can only produce legal sections, harmonic functions and motif transformations.
items.example: A gene chooses between statement-plus-answer and statement-plus-rest; another selects a permitted cadence route.
items.controls: Emotion changes production preferences; energy changes legal density variants; decode against a fixed phrase horizon.
items.failure: Small genotype changes can cause large phenotype changes. Different genes may decode to the same phrase.
items.experiment: Count invalid or duplicate decoded results and compare controllability against direct phrase encoding.

items.title: Differential evolution of composer parameters
items.mechanism: Use population-vector differences to propose continuous parameter candidates.
items.mapping: Search profile parameters such as contour bias, gate ratio and register spread; let a separate decoder realize notes.
items.example: Candidate vectors describe three bounded preferences, not fractional MIDI notes. Decode each with identical evaluation seeds.
items.controls: Energy/emotion supply evaluation scenarios; search completes offline or for a future section, never in a timing callback.
items.failure: Discrete decoding creates plateaus and abrupt jumps. Optimizing one seed overfits incidental choices.
items.experiment: Evaluate across training and held-out control trajectories and compare with a coarse parameter grid.

items.title: Covariance-matrix adaptation evolution strategy
items.mechanism: Adapt a search distribution over continuous parameters, including relationships between parameter directions.
items.mapping: Tune interacting symbolic preferences such as leap size, articulation and rhythmic contrast as a profile-level search.
items.example: A candidate is a five-parameter profile evaluated across several fixed motifs; receiver volume is excluded from the musical objective.
items.controls: Emotion and energy define test contexts; iterations run away from playback; freeze accepted parameters for a session revision.
items.failure: Noisy listener scores and hard quantization can frustrate search. Continuous parameter efficiency does not imply better composition.
items.experiment: Repeat evaluations across seeds and compare with differential evolution using equal decoding budgets.

items.title: Pareto search with NSGA-II
items.mechanism: Maintain candidates trading off multiple objectives through nondominated selection and diversity management.
items.mapping: Keep separate objectives for motif identity, target density and voice-leading instead of hiding their trade-offs in one score.
items.example: A sparse recognizable phrase and a busier less-recognizable phrase can both remain nondominated; choose with the current musical goal.
items.controls: Energy selects a desired region of the frontier; emotion adjusts criteria; time limits when a candidate may be committed.
items.failure: Bad objectives produce a misleading frontier. Many objectives can leave almost everything nondominated.
items.experiment: Inspect representative frontier candidates and validate criteria with musicians rather than reporting frontier size as quality.

items.title: Novelty search
items.mechanism: Select behaviourally unusual candidates relative to neighbours or an archive rather than only a target-performance score.
items.mapping: Define descriptors such as accent position, contour shape and rest distribution for phrase exploration.
items.example: Two phrases with different note names but identical contour and rhythm can be close in the chosen descriptor space.
items.controls: Use novelty as an optional exploration setting; emotion keeps profile eligibility; energy stays an independent activity constraint.
items.failure: Novelty can reward noise, extreme density or trivial transposition if descriptors are poorly chosen.
items.experiment: Compare descriptor novelty with listener-perceived difference and enforce minimum musical validity before archive admission.

items.title: MAP-Elites and quality-diversity libraries
items.mechanism: Keep high-performing candidates in cells of a user-defined behaviour-descriptor space.
items.mapping: Build an auditionable motif library indexed by density and contour, while evaluating validity and identity within each cell.
items.example: A 4-by-4 archive can contain sixteen different density/contour regions. Empty cells indicate missing candidates, not bad music.
items.controls: Energy selects a density region; emotion chooses among compatible colours; section time follows a coherent route through the archive.
items.failure: Descriptor coverage does not establish emotional coverage. Selecting distant cells can destroy continuity.
items.experiment: Inspect archive diversity, transition quality and held-out control following, comparing against an equally sized random library.

items.title: Interactive evolutionary selection
items.mechanism: Use explicit human judgments to help select or rank candidates during an evolutionary process.
items.mapping: Present a small, comparable set of motif variants and let the performer keep, reject or pin material.
items.example: Audition four equal-length phrases under the same renderer; keep two parents and generate a limited next batch.
items.controls: The wheel specifies desired expression; energy is held fixed during a comparison; feedback changes future candidates only.
items.failure: Listening fatigue, order effects and renderer preference can dominate judgments. Frequent interruption undermines autonomous flow.
items.experiment: Measure useful choices per audition, fatigue and later preference stability; offer an offline curation mode.

items.title: Co-evolution of musical parts
items.mechanism: Evaluate evolving populations through their interactions rather than an isolated score for each individual.
items.mapping: Evolve lead and answer candidates together, rewarding complementary rhythm and motif relations within shared budgets.
items.example: A good answer is tested against several lead phrases, so it cannot succeed only by exploiting one partner.
items.controls: Emotion defines shared phrase aims; energy supplies a joint attack budget; selection happens over future phrase ensembles.
items.failure: Populations can cycle or collude toward a simplistic convention. Strong isolated parts may combine poorly.
items.experiment: Test cross-pairings with held-out partners and compare joint evaluation against independently optimized parts.

items.title: Conway’s Game of Life
items.mechanism: On a binary grid, dead cells with three neighbours are born; live cells survive with two or three.
items.mapping: Treat rows as degrees and columns as rhythmic slots. Compare all-live-cell attacks, births-only attacks and persistent-cell sustains.
items.example: A three-cell horizontal blinker becomes vertical after one synchronous step, then horizontal again. These give different rhythmic and harmonic readings.
items.controls: Advance generations on beats or bars. Energy changes the event-selection budget; emotion selects the pitch/articulation mapping, not an assumed biological feeling.
items.failure: Life can freeze, oscillate or die. Torus and dead-edge boundaries behave differently; in-place updates implement a different process.
items.experiment: Verify block, blinker and glider patterns, then compare mappings at equal attack budgets and record every reseed.

items.title: Elementary cellular automata: Rules 30, 90 and 110
items.mechanism: Update a binary line using the three-cell neighbourhood and one of 256 local rule tables.
items.mapping: Read each generation as a rhythmic mask or use one column over time as a part trigger. Map rule outputs through a tonal vocabulary.
items.example: Rule 90 uses left XOR right. A single central live cell produces two live neighbours in its next generation.
items.controls: Time controls generation rate; energy selects a capped number of live slots; emotion can choose mapping and approved rule families.
items.failure: Chaotic appearance is not musical direction. Boundary choice and sampling stride can dominate the audible result.
items.experiment: Check the exact rule table, seed and edge policy; compare several rules with the same symbolic mapping.

items.title: Brian’s Brain
items.mechanism: Use off, firing and refractory states; off cells fire with two firing neighbours, and firing cells become refractory.
items.mapping: Emit attacks only on entry to firing. Refractory states prevent an immediate retrigger at the same location.
items.example: A firing cell is refractory at the next generation and off at the following one; it cannot fire again during the refractory step.
items.controls: Energy controls accepted trigger count; emotion selects contour and gates; retain a generation clock independent from note releases.
items.failure: A births-only rhythm may still become too dense. Treating refractory cells as active neighbours changes the rule.
items.experiment: Verify the state cycle and neighbour counting; compare repeated-note spacing with binary Life at matched density.

items.title: Cyclic cellular automata
items.mechanism: Cells advance through an ordered set of states when neighbourhood conditions favour the next state.
items.mapping: Map state to a motif family or harmonic colour and state changes to attacks, creating moving symbolic waves.
items.example: With states 0,1,2, a cell may advance 2 to 0 when the required neighbouring zeros are present. Specify the threshold and neighbourhood.
items.controls: Energy limits extracted events; emotion selects the state-to-music palette; section time controls when the palette may change.
items.failure: The spatial wave does not supply a cadence. Similar state counts can conceal very different wave geometry.
items.experiment: Compare state occupancy and transition counts with the actual phrase trace; test fixed and wrapped boundaries.

items.title: Generations automata and cellular memory
items.mechanism: Extend Life-like rules with additional decay or history states.
items.mapping: Use cell age to choose articulation or whether a motif is repeated, answered or allowed to fade.
items.example: A trigger entering a four-state cycle can create one attack followed by two silent memory steps rather than three repeated attacks.
items.controls: Energy can select extraction density while decay duration stays stable; emotion changes the interpretation of age.
items.failure: Rule notation may order survival and birth differently from B/S notation. More states do not automatically produce longer musical memory.
items.experiment: Validate rule parsing and age transitions, then compare decay-as-silence with decay-as-sustained-note mappings.

items.title: Reversible block cellular automata
items.mechanism: Apply reversible local transformations on alternating partitions of a grid.
items.mapping: Move a fixed population of rhythmic tokens between slots, conserving material while changing its arrangement.
items.example: A token-swapping block rule preserves the number of tokens; alternate the block origin so tokens can cross previous partition boundaries.
items.controls: Energy selects accents or orchestration rather than silently changing conserved population; emotion selects admissible permutations.
items.failure: Conservation can still yield tedious cycles. A non-bijective rule loses reversibility; note gates must not depend on visual persistence alone.
items.experiment: Run forward then inverse steps and verify state recovery, then measure rhythmic recurrence and useful variation.

items.title: Probabilistic cellular automata
items.mechanism: Use a conditional probability for a cell transition instead of a wholly deterministic rule.
items.mapping: Introduce controlled uncertainty into a rhythmic mask while preserving deterministic anchors outside the grid.
items.example: A candidate birth is accepted with .7 probability keyed by generation and coordinate. Re-querying the same generation must agree.
items.controls: Energy controls the cap independently from birth probability; emotion can choose a validated transition regime.
items.failure: Small probability changes can cause global extinction or explosion. Unkeyed randomness breaks reproducible querying.
items.experiment: Measure survival, density and periodicity over many seeds; label stochastic reseeding separately from ordinary evolution.

items.title: Lenia and continuous cellular automata
items.mechanism: Evolve continuous cell values through neighbourhood kernels and growth functions.
items.mapping: Extract region mass, centroid and movement as slow symbolic register or texture controls, rather than emitting a note from every pixel.
items.example: Quantize a moving centroid to a degree centre once per bar; use total mass to weight a capped set of optional attacks.
items.controls: Time separates simulation step from musical sampling; energy changes extraction limits; emotion chooses the profile mapper.
items.failure: Threshold chatter and numerical instability can dominate. A continuous visual organism is not evidence of expressive musical behaviour.
items.experiment: Check bounded finite states and sampling-rate sensitivity; compare regional features with raw threshold crossings.

items.title: Gray–Scott reaction-diffusion
items.mechanism: Couple local reaction and spatial diffusion of two concentration fields.
items.mapping: Use connected regions and threshold-crossing fronts to create phrase activity or spatially organized symbolic voices.
items.example: Sample four fixed regions at phrase boundaries and assign each an activity rank. Avoid turning thousands of simulation cells into simultaneous notes.
items.controls: Energy bounds active musical regions; emotion selects register and articulation; feed/kill changes are slow experimental controls.
items.failure: Simulation parameters have nonlinear regime changes. A stable visual pattern may produce static musical output.
items.experiment: Test numerical stability, region extraction and density caps before comparing musical trajectories with simple envelopes.

items.title: Langton-style ant and mobile automata
items.mechanism: An agent reads a cell state, turns, changes that state and moves according to a fixed local rule.
items.mapping: Use turns as interval directions and visited cells as rhythm or motif-memory locations.
items.example: For a specified two-colour rule, alternate left/right turning according to the current colour; the same seed and rule reproduce the path.
items.controls: Energy changes extraction rate or accents, not secretly simulation speed; emotion maps turns into allowed contour vocabulary.
items.failure: Long transients and repeated highways can dominate output. Boundary wrapping materially changes future visits.
items.experiment: Replay exact coordinates and compare turn-to-contour with location-to-pitch mappings under identical event counts.

items.title: Context-free musical grammars
items.mechanism: Expand nonterminal symbols through production rules until a terminal structure is obtained.
items.mapping: Let phrases expand into statement, response and cadence cells, each carrying a known duration and harmonic contract.
items.example: Phrase -> Statement Response Cadence; assign durations 4,2,2 beats so the result fills eight beats exactly.
items.controls: Emotion chooses legal terminal variants; energy chooses ornamented variants; depth and duration constrain expansion.
items.failure: Recursive productions can fail to terminate or expand beyond the intended duration. Valid syntax is not convincing phrasing.
items.experiment: Check termination, duration sums and join conditions; compare generated forms with authored sequences.

items.title: Probabilistic context-free grammars
items.mechanism: Attach normalized choice probabilities to alternative productions.
items.mapping: Vary phrase structures while retaining the same hierarchical musical roles and terminal constraints.
items.example: A response may expand to Echo with .6 probability or Contrast with .4. Its selected production still must meet the duration contract.
items.controls: The wheel modifies profile-specific production weights; energy selects surface complexity; section position conditions ending rules.
items.failure: High recursion probability can create excessive depth. Probability-weighted syntax does not ensure balanced large-scale form.
items.experiment: Measure realized production frequencies, termination and phrase lengths before listening to structural diversity.

items.title: Deterministic L-systems
items.mechanism: Rewrite all symbols in parallel using fixed productions.
items.mapping: Interpret the resulting string as interval moves, rests and rhythmic cells; keep the derivation separate from musical mapping.
items.example: With A->AB and B->A, successive strings are A, AB, ABA, ABAAB. Map A and B to distinct authored cells.
items.controls: Generation controls structural scale; energy controls selected realizations; emotion selects the A/B musical vocabulary.
items.failure: String length can grow rapidly. Plant-like or fractal structure does not automatically become recognizable musical form.
items.experiment: Verify derivation lengths and token mapping; compare repeated generations at constant total duration.

items.title: Stochastic L-systems
items.mechanism: Choose among parallel rewrite alternatives with declared probabilities.
items.mapping: Generate related phrase families whose branching structures vary without replacing the whole motif vocabulary.
items.example: A may become AB with .7 probability or BA with .3; use independent keyed choices for each symbol instance.
items.controls: Emotion shifts bounded production weights; energy controls allowed terminal density; derivation depth is fixed per planned section.
items.failure: Structural randomness can erase the seed theme. A mutable random stream makes results depend on traversal order.
items.experiment: Compare motif resemblance and derivation diversity across seeds, with exact duration normalization.

items.title: Context-sensitive rewriting
items.mechanism: Choose a rewrite using neighbouring symbols as well as the symbol being replaced.
items.mapping: Make a response depend on surrounding harmonic or phrase-role tokens, allowing locally aware development.
items.example: Rewrite an ornament token differently when preceded by a dominant marker than when preceded by a tonic marker.
items.controls: Emotion modifies allowed response rules; energy sets ornament budgets; evaluate each generation against the same frozen context.
items.failure: Overlapping matches need precedence rules. Updating symbols in place accidentally changes parallel rewrite semantics.
items.experiment: Use small hand-derived strings to check matching and compare context-aware joins with context-free ones.

items.title: Parametric L-systems
items.mechanism: Carry numerical parameters on symbols and transform them through production expressions.
items.mapping: Attach degree offset, duration and accent to motif cells, enabling gradual growth or contraction.
items.example: A cell F(d,t) can expand to F(d,t/2) followed by F(d+2,t/2), preserving total duration while adding movement.
items.controls: Energy bounds subdivision; emotion controls allowed degree changes; section time fixes recursion depth.
items.failure: Duration can shrink below playable limits. Parameter growth may push register outside the profile.
items.experiment: Check total duration, minimum gate and pitch bounds at every derivation, not only after final decoding.

items.title: Graph grammars for form
items.mechanism: Rewrite subgraphs according to rules while retaining declared connections.
items.mapping: Expand a section graph into statement, contrast and return structures with explicit incoming and outgoing harmonic conditions.
items.example: Replace one development node with two linked variants while keeping its entrance and exit nodes unchanged.
items.controls: Emotion changes eligible expansions; energy changes orchestration inside nodes; form edits affect future sections only.
items.failure: Rewrites can introduce unreachable endings or cycles. Graph validity alone does not make transitions audible.
items.experiment: Check reachability and bounded duration, then compare the heard form with its planned graph.

items.title: Petri-net-inspired musical coordination
items.mechanism: Tokens enable transitions subject to input and output conditions.
items.mapping: Represent available musical roles or turn-taking permissions as tokens, so an answer begins only after its lead phrase has yielded.
items.example: A lead-finished token and a harmony-ready token jointly enable an answer transition; firing consumes the permission and starts the response.
items.controls: Energy controls optional transitions; emotion selects response vocabulary; musical time controls transition deadlines.
items.failure: Deadlock, token accumulation and starvation are musical failures as well as formal ones. A timeout needs an explicit rest/fallback policy.
items.experiment: Trace token conservation and reachability on interrupted phrases, then assess whether turn-taking sounds intentional.

items.title: Finite-state arrangement machines
items.mechanism: Use explicit states and guarded transitions to control behaviour.
items.mapping: Define sparse, moving, intense and closing textures, each with part permissions and minimum residence time.
items.example: Enter intense above energy .7 and leave below .5; a separate finish request moves toward closing at the next valid boundary.
items.controls: Energy drives guarded transitions; emotion changes state realization; elapsed bars enforce residence and ending reachability.
items.failure: Threshold flicker and unreachable states create unstable arrangements. State names should not claim measured human emotions.
items.experiment: Exercise threshold crossings, rapid controls and finish requests; compare against an unguarded threshold controller.

items.title: Behaviour trees for a musical conductor
items.mechanism: Compose conditions and actions through success, failure and running states.
items.mapping: Prioritize Stop, cadence obligations, human turn-taking and optional development through a readable decision tree.
items.example: Try satisfy-ending first; otherwise preserve-human-lead; otherwise choose one developmental action. Running actions retain their state.
items.controls: Emotion affects action preferences; energy affects budgets; the tree ticks at planning boundaries, not for every audio sample.
items.failure: A tree can repeatedly restart an action or starve lower priorities. Running-state cancellation must release owned notes.
items.experiment: Log branches and cancellation paths; compare decisions against a fixed scenario set and musician annotations.

items.title: Logistic-map control
items.mechanism: Iterate x_next=r*x*(1-x), whose behaviour depends strongly on r and the initial condition.
items.mapping: Map a bounded trajectory to phrase-level accent or motif-choice preferences, then apply musical constraints.
items.example: For r=4 and x=.2, the next value is .64 and then .9216. Repeated rounding to notes can hide much of the trajectory.
items.controls: Time sets iteration versus musical sampling; energy sets output range; emotion chooses a mapper rather than an asserted chaos-to-feeling rule.
items.failure: Finite precision and exceptional seeds can produce periodic or degenerate output. More chaotic parameters do not guarantee more energy.
items.experiment: Record seed, precision and sampling stride; compare with uniform and correlated random controls.

items.title: Henon-map symbolic control
items.mechanism: Iterate a two-dimensional nonlinear map, conventionally x_next=1-a*x*x+y and y_next=b*x.
items.mapping: Map two related coordinates to contour centre and rhythmic-cell preference, using measured normalization bounds.
items.example: Compute both next coordinates from the old state. Updating y from the new x changes the map.
items.controls: Energy bounds emitted activity; emotion selects allowed cells; sample at declared beat or bar intervals.
items.failure: Some parameters diverge; attractor shape does not establish musical form. Fixed min-max assumptions can clip rare excursions.
items.experiment: Check finite bounded trajectories and coordinate-update order before testing heard correlation between musical dimensions.

items.title: Lorenz-system trajectories
items.mechanism: Integrate coupled nonlinear differential equations to obtain a time-varying trajectory.
items.mapping: Use changes between broad trajectory regions as section cues and one coordinate as a bounded register preference.
items.example: Sample a normalized coordinate once per bar rather than translating every solver step into a note. Store solver settings for replay.
items.controls: Energy affects musical extraction; emotion maps regions to phrase vocabularies; simulation and transport time remain distinct.
items.failure: Integration step and initial state affect outcomes. Chaotic divergence makes regenerated long sessions sensitive to numerical implementation.
items.experiment: Compare integration tolerances and save resolved symbolic traces; test whether region changes support useful musical transitions.

items.title: Circle maps and modular phase processes
items.mechanism: Iterate an angular state modulo one, optionally with nonlinear phase feedback.
items.mapping: Use phase crossing as an attack source and phase differences as rhythmic relationships between parts.
items.example: The simple rotation theta_next=(theta+1/3) mod 1 repeats after three steps; an irrational increment has different recurrence behaviour.
items.controls: Energy can alter extraction density while preserving reference tempo; emotion adjusts accents and permitted phrase roles.
items.failure: Floating-point equality is unsuitable for detecting wrap events. Nonlinear parameters can produce unexpected locking regimes.
items.experiment: Count crossings from unwrapped phase and compare rational and irrational rotations under finite precision.

items.title: Coupled phase oscillators and Kuramoto networks
items.mechanism: Let oscillator phases influence one another through a coupling function.
items.mapping: Assign parts to oscillators and trigger symbolic gestures at phase crossings, allowing alignment and divergence.
items.example: Two close frequencies may align more strongly as coupling increases; extract event times through crossing detection, not display frames.
items.controls: Energy controls orchestration; emotion can select coupling profiles; a master transport still governs delivery and phrase boundaries.
items.failure: Synchronization can reduce interesting variation. Numerical steps can miss crossings, and abrupt coupling changes can disrupt phrasing.
items.experiment: Measure phase coherence and event timing separately; compare emergent alignment with an authored polymetric cycle.

items.title: Iterated function systems
items.mechanism: Repeatedly apply selected transformations to a state, often using contractive maps.
items.mapping: Generate self-related register and duration preferences, then resolve them into a finite phrase vocabulary.
items.example: Select between two bounded affine transformations and map the resulting coordinate to one of seven degree regions.
items.controls: Emotion selects transform weights; energy controls attack budgets; iteration depth and musical sampling are independent.
items.failure: Visually self-similar structure may disappear after quantization. Non-contractive choices can diverge.
items.experiment: Compare latent and realized recurrence, verify boundedness and audition against simple recursive motif transformations.

items.title: Recursive and fractal rhythmic subdivision
items.mechanism: Recursively replace a time span with smaller spans according to a fixed rule.
items.mapping: Create nested phrase rhythm while preserving total duration and selected anchor positions.
items.example: Split four beats into [2,2], then split only the second half into [1,1], giving onset spans [0,2,3].
items.controls: Energy chooses maximum depth or eligible subdivisions; emotion chooses long-short organization; section position protects cadential space.
items.failure: Deep recursion produces unplayably short gates and too many attacks. Fractal terminology does not itself explain a listening benefit.
items.experiment: Check duration conservation and minimum event spacing; compare nested and flat patterns at equal density.

items.title: Thue–Morse substitution sequences
items.mechanism: Apply 0->01 and 1->10 repeatedly to construct a structured nonperiodic infinite word.
items.mapping: Use symbols to alternate two motif realizations, accent families or instrumental roles.
items.example: The first eight symbols are 01101001. Map 0 to an original cell and 1 to a bounded inversion.
items.controls: Energy changes realization, not the sequence identity; emotion chooses the paired cells; group symbols into explicit phrases.
items.failure: Nonperiodicity is not randomness or endless novelty. A two-cell vocabulary can remain perceptually repetitive.
items.experiment: Verify prefixes and compare heard motif development against ordinary alternating and random binary schedules.

items.title: Fibonacci words and unequal recurrence
items.mechanism: Use the substitution A->AB, B->A to create a structured symbol sequence.
items.mapping: Assign A and B different rhythmic cells or section gestures to vary return intervals.
items.example: A, AB, ABA and ABAAB contain lengths 1,2,3,5. If cell durations differ, symbol count is not elapsed musical time.
items.controls: Energy selects cell realizations; emotion selects compatible colours; the conductor groups the sequence into phrase-sized windows.
items.failure: Irrational limiting proportions do not ensure a useful groove. Window boundaries can cut cells or obscure cadences.
items.experiment: Check symbol and duration growth separately and compare proportional versus metric grouping.

items.title: De Bruijn sequences
items.mechanism: Arrange symbols cyclically so every word of a fixed length occurs once.
items.mapping: Systematically audition local rhythmic or motif-choice combinations without independent random repetition.
items.example: The cyclic binary sequence 00010111 contains each three-bit word once when wraparound windows are included.
items.controls: Energy maps symbols to different activity levels; emotion selects material; cycle traversal is grouped into musically planned sections.
items.failure: Exhaustive local coverage is not convincing long-range form. Mapping collisions can make distinct words sound identical.
items.experiment: Verify unique cyclic windows and compare perceived variety with a matched-length random sequence.

items.title: Boids and flocking
items.mechanism: Combine local separation, alignment and cohesion rules for moving agents.
items.mapping: Map agent height to register and group alignment to shared rhythmic direction; keep each agent assigned to a bounded musical role.
items.example: Three agents converge in contour direction while separation prevents them all selecting the same register slot.
items.controls: Emotion chooses attraction targets and phrase vocabulary; energy controls accepted attacks; time schedules sampled states.
items.failure: Physical closeness is not harmonic consonance. Mapping every simulation step to an attack creates overwhelming output.
items.experiment: Compare collective motion features with actual interval and rhythm relationships at a fixed polyphony cap.

items.title: Ant-colony-inspired phrase routing
items.mechanism: Reinforce promising graph routes with a decaying shared trail.
items.mapping: Let candidate agents explore chord or motif routes, depositing bounded preference on routes meeting phrase goals.
items.example: A route resolving a cadence receives trail reinforcement, while evaporation prevents its edges from permanently dominating.
items.controls: Energy changes rhythm realization; emotion changes route desirability; exploration runs before phrase commitment.
items.failure: Early random advantages can become lock-in. Trail strength is an internal search signal, not a judgment of artistic value.
items.experiment: Compare route diversity and target attainment with ordinary weighted graph walks at the same evaluation budget.

items.title: Particle swarm optimization
items.mechanism: Move candidate parameter vectors using their own and neighbours’ best-known positions.
items.mapping: Search a continuous composer-control space offline, with a fixed symbolic decoder and several evaluation scenarios.
items.example: Particles tune contour bias and rhythmic contrast; the best parameter vector still needs to be decoded and auditioned.
items.controls: Emotion and energy define target scenarios; time supplies a search deadline, not the particle integration rate for playback.
items.failure: Particles can collapse prematurely or exploit a noisy evaluator. PSO is optimization, distinct from performing a flock simulation.
items.experiment: Compare with equal-budget random and differential-evolution searches using held-out seeds.

items.title: Predator–prey musical populations
items.mechanism: Couple populations through growth, resource use and predation or an analogous interaction.
items.mapping: Map slowly changing populations to competing phrase textures, not individual animal-like notes.
items.example: A rising ornament population increases activity while a suppressor population later thins it, producing an experimental long arc.
items.controls: Energy caps realized notes independently of population; emotion changes mapping; freeze the simulation-to-bar time scale.
items.failure: Extinction, runaway growth and numerical oscillation may dominate. An ecological metaphor does not supply harmonic meaning.
items.experiment: Check positivity and boundedness, then compare the activity arc with a deliberately authored rise-and-fall envelope.

items.title: Replicator dynamics for strategy mixtures
items.mechanism: Change strategy proportions according to relative payoff in a population.
items.mapping: Let repeat, answer and transform strategies compete for future phrase selection using explicit, inspectable payoffs.
items.example: A strategy gaining share is used more often, but one strategy is sampled per opportunity rather than all firing concurrently.
items.controls: Emotion changes payoff hypotheses; energy constrains realization; update proportions only after committed phrases.
items.failure: Payoff design can erase diversity or generate cycles. A successful strategy can mean metric exploitation rather than musical quality.
items.experiment: Track population shares, cycles and listener judgments; compare against a fixed authored strategy mixture.

items.title: Sandpile and avalanche processes
items.mechanism: Accumulate local quantities and redistribute them when a specified threshold is exceeded.
items.mapping: Use avalanches as candidates for short fills or orchestrational cascades, bounded by a phrase event budget.
items.example: Adding one token can trigger several topplings; map only a summarized avalanche size and path to one bounded musical gesture.
items.controls: Energy sets a fill budget; emotion chooses gesture vocabulary; defer cascades to eligible musical slots.
items.failure: Unbounded avalanches can exceed deadlines. A finite simulation does not automatically establish self-organized criticality.
items.experiment: Record size and duration distributions; compare against directly sampled fill sizes before claiming a benefit.

items.title: Diffusion-limited aggregation
items.mechanism: Random walkers attach to an existing cluster under a declared contact rule.
items.mapping: Use a growing graph as a motif genealogy or source of branching phrase routes.
items.example: Each attached branch inherits its parent motif and adds one small transformation; sample one path for a phrase.
items.controls: Emotion selects transformation vocabulary; energy sets active branches; growth steps are separate from beat time.
items.failure: Large trees cost memory and can have unhelpful long branches. Growth geometry does not by itself create audible genealogy.
items.experiment: Verify bounded growth and provenance, then test whether listeners recognize parent-child motif relationships.

items.title: Excitable and refractory networks
items.mechanism: Nodes activate in response to input and then pass through a refractory interval.
items.mapping: Model a network of answering motifs where one gesture can invite another after a known delay.
items.example: A lead activation enables an answer node; its refractory period prevents immediate repeated answers.
items.controls: Energy controls transmission eligibility; emotion selects response cells; delays are expressed in musical beats.
items.failure: Feedback loops can create uncontrolled activity. A refractory rule needs clear units and deterministic update order.
items.experiment: Test pulse propagation, loop termination and density bounds, then compare with a simple call-and-response state machine.

items.title: Stigmergic shared musical memory
items.mechanism: Coordinate agents indirectly through persistent, decaying changes in a shared environment.
items.mapping: Let performed motifs leave tagged traces that bias later answers without a direct instruction from the original part.
items.example: A phrase leaves an interval-contour trace for four bars; an answering part may recall it, while decay prevents endless reuse.
items.controls: Emotion affects trace compatibility; energy controls answer opportunities; trace age uses committed musical time.
items.failure: Shared traces can become an echo chamber. Speculative generation must not leave traces for music never performed.
items.experiment: Track provenance and expiry; compare indirect recall with explicit conductor-selected memory.

items.title: Resource auctions and role allocation
items.mechanism: Allocate limited resources among agents through an explicit bidding or priority mechanism.
items.mapping: Treat foreground slots, register space and attack budgets as resources requested by musical parts.
items.example: The lead requests a phrase-ending slot and outranks an optional counterline; an aged unserved answer can gain priority later.
items.controls: Energy sets total resources; emotion affects eligible roles; allocation happens at phrase boundaries.
items.failure: Poor priority rules can starve a part or always privilege dense generators. Winning is not an aesthetic proof.
items.experiment: Inspect allocations, starvation and heard foreground clarity against an independent-part baseline.

items.title: Constraint programming for musical events
items.mechanism: Assign variables from finite domains subject to explicit relationships.
items.mapping: Solve a short phrase with pitch ranges, chord anchors, duration totals and voice-separation requirements.
items.example: Choose four degree anchors from finite sets while requiring the last anchor to reach the cadence target and total rhythm to fill the bar.
items.controls: Emotion adds soft preferences; energy sets hard event budgets; solve before the phrase deadline.
items.failure: An infeasible model needs a diagnostic and fallback. Hard-coding one style’s rules can exclude intended expression.
items.experiment: Check solutions and infeasible examples; record which preferences were relaxed and compare with musician annotations.

items.title: SAT/SMT-style symbolic composition
items.mechanism: Express decisions through logical variables and satisfiability constraints.
items.mapping: Represent whether a note occupies a slot, whether a voice crosses another and whether a prepared dissonance resolves.
items.example: An implication can state that an accented non-chord event requires a suitable resolution in one of the next two slots.
items.controls: Emotion selects permitted obligations; energy bounds active slots; use a finite phrase horizon.
items.failure: Boolean encoding can become large. A satisfiable assignment can remain musically dull; SMT and SAT solver contracts differ.
items.experiment: Use hand-checkable miniature scores and contrast satisfiability with independent musical-quality evaluation.

items.title: Mixed-integer and integer programming
items.mechanism: Optimize an objective under linear relationships with integer and optionally continuous decision variables.
items.mapping: Allocate onsets, parts and register placements to meet a global density plan and minimize declared movement costs.
items.example: Binary slot variables sum to six optional attacks; continuous variables can describe some performance preferences in a suitable solver.
items.controls: Energy sets occupancy bounds; emotion changes objective weights; time supplies a deadline and feasible fallback.
items.failure: Some musical rules need nonlinear or expanded encodings. CP-SAT specifically uses integer terms, not arbitrary continuous variables.
items.experiment: Compare feasible incumbents at a fixed time budget and inspect objective components rather than claiming global musical optimality.

items.title: Dynamic programming for phrase paths
items.mechanism: Reuse solutions to subproblems when the retained state contains all information needed for future costs.
items.mapping: Select a sequence of voicings or melodic anchors with minimal declared transition cost over a fixed harmonic route.
items.example: For each chord and candidate voicing, store the best predecessor cost and reconstruct the final path.
items.controls: Emotion supplies candidate vocabulary; energy constrains texture; phrase length fixes the planning horizon.
items.failure: A state omitting unresolved suspensions or motif position loses necessary history. More state increases cost.
items.experiment: Compare with exhaustive search on tiny cases and audition against greedy nearest-voicing selection.

items.title: Shortest-path composition
items.mechanism: Find a route through a weighted graph under the selected algorithm’s cost assumptions.
items.mapping: Treat harmonic or pitch-set states as vertices and admissible transitions as edges.
items.example: Find a route from an opening chord to a cadence through two intermediate layers, with edges weighted by voice movement.
items.controls: Emotion selects graph regions; energy alters realization; time-layered vertices can enforce exact phrase length.
items.failure: The cheapest route can be repetitive or too short. Negative costs and cycles require the correct algorithm and interpretation.
items.experiment: Verify route length and edge costs; compare the resulting music with alternative near-optimal routes.

items.title: Beam search
items.mechanism: Keep only a bounded number of promising partial sequences at each expansion step.
items.mapping: Build phrases with several possible future continuations while limiting computation.
items.example: A width-four beam retains four partial motifs after each note; score obligations and remaining cadence reachability before pruning.
items.controls: Emotion changes candidate ranking; energy limits expansions; commit only complete validated phrases.
items.failure: An early scoring bias can eliminate the best long-term route. Beam width does not remove a flawed objective.
items.experiment: Compare widths and equal-budget random proposals, tracking both completion failures and musical preferences.

items.title: A-star musical planning
items.mechanism: Prioritize partial routes using accumulated cost plus an estimate of remaining cost.
items.mapping: Plan a harmonic or motif-transformation route to a known future target.
items.example: A lower bound on remaining pitch movement can guide a constrained approach to a cadence; artistic surprise is evaluated separately.
items.controls: Emotion chooses the target region; energy constrains realization; search has a bounded musical horizon.
items.failure: Optimality claims require the relevant heuristic conditions. A perceptual cost estimate may be useful but not admissible.
items.experiment: Check tiny graph solutions against exhaustive search and distinguish formal path optimality from perceived musical success.

items.title: Monte Carlo tree search
items.mechanism: Allocate exploration to a decision tree through repeated selection, expansion and evaluated simulations.
items.mapping: Explore a few phrase-level conductor actions by simulating their symbolic consequences over a short horizon.
items.example: Compare hold, thin and introduce-answer actions through bounded rollouts; none of the hypothetical notes is sent to output.
items.controls: Emotion supplies goals; energy sets budgets; planning time limits rollouts before the commitment boundary.
items.failure: A poor rollout evaluator can prefer harmful actions. Simulated future audience satisfaction is not an observed reward.
items.experiment: Compare with exhaustive shallow action evaluation and count decision quality per computation budget.

items.title: Wave Function Collapse for musical tiles
items.mechanism: Propagate local compatibility constraints while selecting among remaining tile possibilities.
items.mapping: Use authored rhythmic/harmonic cells as tiles with entry, exit and voice-leading compatibility labels.
items.example: A dominant-entry tile can only follow a compatible predecessor; pin a cadence tile at the final slot and propagate constraints backward.
items.controls: Emotion adjusts tile weights; energy selects permitted densities; time fixes finite phrase length.
items.failure: Local compatibility does not guarantee long-form development. Contradictions need bounded backtracking or restart; this is not quantum computation.
items.experiment: Test impossible tile sets, completion rate and phrase joins against simple compatible random concatenation.

items.title: Simulated annealing
items.mechanism: Explore local changes while sometimes accepting worse objective values according to a cooling schedule.
items.mapping: Refine a valid phrase by changing optional pitches, durations or voicings while protecting anchor obligations.
items.example: Try shifting one inner note by a degree; evaluate movement and contour costs before deciding whether to keep the change.
items.controls: Emotion defines the profile objective; energy remains a bound; cooling runs before playback or on future phrases.
items.failure: A low objective is not artistic quality. Discrete moves and a continuous library implementation require a deliberate adapter.
items.experiment: Compare with greedy local search at equal proposal counts and preserve the best feasible phrase as fallback.

items.title: Euclidean and maximally even rhythms
items.mechanism: Distribute a selected number of onsets as evenly as possible around a cycle.
items.mapping: Build rhythm scaffolds, then separately choose rotation, accents, pitches and gates.
items.example: Three attacks in eight slots can be x..x..x.; rotating by one slot gives .x..x..x, changing metric placement without changing count.
items.controls: Energy selects onset count; emotion selects accent and contour; preserve phrase-scale changes above the rhythmic cycle.
items.failure: Binary evenness does not reproduce a cultural performance practice. Different rotation conventions can cause unexpected alignment.
items.experiment: Check attack counts and cyclic gaps, then compare accents and rotations at constant density.

items.title: Polymetric loop composition
items.mechanism: Run musical cycles with different lengths against a common time unit.
items.mapping: Use a short bass loop and a differently sized answer cycle to create changing alignments.
items.example: Loops of three and four equal-duration steps realign after twelve steps. Their harmony still needs coordination.
items.controls: Energy changes orchestration rather than cycle lengths by default; emotion selects material; time tracks the supercycle.
items.failure: Independent loops can conflict at harmonic changes. Least common multiple in steps is not valid when step durations differ.
items.experiment: Verify alignment and chord-boundary handling; compare changing alignments with an authored twelve-step arrangement.

items.title: Discrete and gradual phase shifting
items.mechanism: Change the relative temporal offset between related repeating material.
items.mapping: Keep a motif recognizable while a second realization moves through new attack relationships.
items.example: Delay one four-beat motif by half a beat while preserving the master pulse; distinguish this discrete shift from a temporary tempo difference.
items.controls: Energy controls entrances and accents; emotion selects interval treatment; phase movement occurs over an explicit duration.
items.failure: Crossings can overcrowd the arrangement. Tempo-based drift needs a reunification and note-release policy.
items.experiment: Compare fixed-offset, stepped and gradual shifts at matched material and assess recognizable return.

items.title: Isorhythmic pitch-duration pairing
items.mechanism: Repeat pitch and duration sequences independently so their pairings evolve.
items.mapping: Use a short pitch cell with a differently sized duration cell to generate limited-material variation.
items.example: A three-pitch sequence and five-duration sequence repeat their pairings after fifteen events, not necessarily fifteen beats.
items.controls: Energy selects duration vocabulary; emotion changes pitch-cell realization; section time decides where to interrupt or resolve.
items.failure: Event-count recurrence can cross bar boundaries. Changing durations changes the elapsed supercycle length.
items.experiment: Calculate both pair recurrence and actual summed duration; compare phrase endings with and without conductor intervention.

items.title: Canon and delayed imitation
items.mechanism: Derive another voice by a specified time delay and pitch or contour transformation.
items.mapping: Compose a source phrase with its answer in mind, retaining explicit provenance between voices.
items.example: A theme delayed two beats and transposed a diatonic fifth becomes an answer only if range and current harmony permit it.
items.controls: Energy controls active imitation voices; emotion chooses transformations; delay stays in declared beat units.
items.failure: A delayed line can collide with a later chord or obscure the source. Heavy repair should be labelled free imitation.
items.experiment: Check exact derivation before repair and evaluate voice independence and intelligibility after repair.

items.title: Serial rows and ordered pitch-class operations
items.mechanism: Transform an ordered pitch-class collection through transposition, inversion, retrograde and related operations.
items.mapping: Use a row as pitch-order structure while rhythm, register and articulation remain separate decisions.
items.example: For row fragment [0,1,4], inversion around zero gives [0,11,8] modulo twelve. Assign register afterward.
items.controls: Emotion selects realization preferences, not an automatic tonal label; energy controls rhythm; phrase time controls row segmentation.
items.failure: Ordered coverage does not supply convincing form. Tonal chord-fit metrics can misjudge the intended profile.
items.experiment: Verify row transformations and repeated pitch classes, then compare heard relatedness under controlled rhythm and register.

items.title: Constrained motif permutations
items.mechanism: Reorder motif events or cells while preserving declared invariants.
items.mapping: Keep first and last anchors and permute only interior cells, retaining a phrase’s entry and ending contracts.
items.example: For four cells A,B,C,D, preserve A and D and compare A-B-C-D with A-C-B-D.
items.controls: Energy selects ornament realization; emotion weights admissible permutations; change only at a planned phrase boundary.
items.failure: A permutation can destroy contour or prepared dissonance. Distinct symbolic orders can sound nearly identical.
items.experiment: Verify preserved anchors and obligations, then assess listener recognition and join quality.

items.title: Tintinnabuli-inspired constrained pairing
items.mechanism: Pair a melodic line with pitches selected by a declared triadic relationship.
items.mapping: Create an experimental companion voice that chooses the nearest eligible triad tone above or below each melodic pitch.
items.example: Against C-major triad classes, D4 can pair with E4 under an above-nearest rule or C4 under a below-nearest rule.
items.controls: Emotion chooses the companion rule and triad vocabulary; energy controls entry and gate; harmony remains explicit.
items.failure: This simplified proposal does not reproduce a composer’s full practice. Constant pairing can create excessive homorhythm.
items.experiment: Check directional selection and compare paired voices with independent counterlines at equal polyphony.

items.title: Voice-leading and voicing optimization
items.mechanism: Select pitch placements for chord identities according to movement, range, spacing and voice relationships.
items.mapping: Enumerate bounded voicing candidates and optimize across several chords, preserving a separate bass function.
items.example: C-E-G to C-E-A retains two common tones, unlike moving every voice to a high root-position A-minor chord.
items.controls: Energy alters spacing or role count; emotion changes eligible harmonies; time fixes chord-change positions.
items.failure: Minimum movement can become static. Independent sorting can hide voice identity or crossing.
items.experiment: Compare greedy and phrase-level paths and inspect individual voices as well as summed movement.

items.title: Transformational harmony graphs
items.mechanism: Represent chords as nodes connected by specified musical transformations.
items.mapping: Traverse a graph of common-tone-preserving or profile-defined chord relationships while preserving a thematic rhythm.
items.example: Move C major to A minor through a two-common-tone relation; label the relationship rather than assuming every edge has equal expressive meaning.
items.controls: Emotion biases relationship families; energy affects texture; section time sets targets and return obligations.
items.failure: Graph adjacency is not a universal harmonic grammar. A route can wander indefinitely without a planned return.
items.experiment: Check edge definitions and audible transitions, comparing constrained routes with functional-harmony plans.

items.title: Recurrent and LSTM note models
items.mechanism: Generate a sequence using a recurrent hidden state conditioned on previous events.
items.mapping: Propose a melody continuation from recent resolved notes and the planned harmony, with a procedural fallback.
items.example: A worker receives two bars of symbolic context and proposes the next phrase; reject it if its plan revision is obsolete.
items.controls: Emotion conditions or reranks proposals only where supported; energy is verified in the resolved score; generation has a deadline.
items.failure: Local continuation can lose form and identity. A sampling temperature is not a calibrated emotion or energy control.
items.experiment: Compare held-out continuation, motif retention, actual control following and deadline failures separately.

items.title: Symbolic Transformer models
items.mechanism: Use attention over tokenized musical context to predict or reconstruct symbolic events.
items.mapping: Propose longer motif-aware continuations while explicit plans retain section, harmony and ending authority.
items.example: Represent time, pitch and duration explicitly; preserve a theme reference in context and validate the decoded note lifecycle.
items.controls: Emotion needs actual conditioning or constrained reranking; energy is measured from the output; plan ahead outside delivery callbacks.
items.failure: Context length does not guarantee controllability or long-form quality. Tokenization can lose voice or meter information.
items.experiment: Compare early and late excerpts, locked-region preservation and training-fragment similarity under documented data provenance.

items.title: Variational autoencoders for motifs
items.mechanism: Encode musical sequences into a latent distribution and decode samples or interpolated latent values.
items.mapping: Create related phrase variants for an authored theme, keeping selected rhythm or cadence anchors protected.
items.example: Decode several points between two motif latents and inspect whether pitch contour changes smoothly after symbolic quantization.
items.controls: Emotion may choose calibrated latent regions; energy stays an explicit checked descriptor; transitions occur at phrase boundaries.
items.failure: Latent distance is not perceptual distance. Interpolation may lose motif identity or violate locked material.
items.experiment: Evaluate reconstruction, variation and controllability separately; compare with simple rule-based motif transforms.

items.title: Generative adversarial models for symbolic tracks
items.mechanism: Train a generator against a discriminator over symbolic representations such as multitrack piano rolls.
items.mapping: Propose coordinated short textures or accompaniment candidates, then convert them into explicit note events.
items.example: A five-track piano roll needs a defined rule for repeated adjacent cells, sustained gates and overlapping voices before MIDI delivery.
items.controls: Emotion and energy require supported conditions or post-selection; time reserves a bounded candidate window.
items.failure: Piano-roll plausibility is not complete song form. Mode collapse can hide behind attractive selected demos.
items.experiment: Inspect diversity, note decoding and interpart relationships alongside listener ratings and rejected examples.

items.title: Diffusion models for symbolic scores
items.mechanism: Iteratively denoise a symbolic or latent representation, potentially conditioned on higher-level structure.
items.mapping: Generate future phrases under form, harmony and texture conditions while preserving fixed regions.
items.example: Freeze an authored theme and ask for accompaniment in the remaining symbolic regions; verify that fixed material is unchanged.
items.controls: Emotion enters only through supported controls; energy is checked after decoding; iteration count must meet the planning deadline.
items.failure: Guidance strength is not musical correctness. Denoising may be too slow for an immediate response.
items.experiment: Measure edit locality, structure following and generation delay against the procedural baseline.

items.title: Retrieval-augmented symbolic composition
items.mechanism: Retrieve relevant source fragments and transform or combine them for the current context.
items.mapping: Search a provenance-preserving library by contour, rhythm, harmonic role and user-approved tags.
items.example: Retrieve an answering cell with the same ending function, transpose it deliberately and trim only within its declared duration contract.
items.controls: Emotion biases tags as hypotheses; energy filters density; time chooses eligible phrase roles and recency.
items.failure: Similarity is not quality, and retrieval can repeat sources too literally. Source licensing and attribution remain separate questions.
items.experiment: Compare retrieval relevance, join quality and motif repetition against authored random cell selection.

items.title: Reservoir and echo-state sequence models
items.mechanism: Use a recurrent dynamical reservoir with a trained readout to model temporal relationships.
items.mapping: Predict a small set of motif or rhythmic states rather than directly controlling every MIDI byte.
items.example: Feed recent interval/rhythm features into a fixed reservoir and train a bounded next-cell classifier, then let the conductor choose among proposals.
items.controls: Emotion and energy can be explicit input features with tested coverage; state resets occur at declared boundaries.
items.failure: Reservoir stability and memory depend on design. Unseen control combinations may produce unreliable predictions.
items.experiment: Compare with a small Markov baseline and test resets, long rests and held-out control trajectories.

items.title: Reinforcement learning for conductor actions
items.mechanism: Learn an action policy through transitions and rewards in a specified environment.
items.mapping: Choose bounded actions such as hold, answer, thin or return; keep event validation and transport ownership deterministic.
items.example: Reward valid cadence completion and explicit task success while retaining separate penalties for excessive density and ignored human input.
items.controls: The wheel is part of the observed context; energy sets action limits; training simulation is separate from live execution.
items.failure: Reward hacking and simulator mismatch can dominate. A handcrafted reward is not measured listener satisfaction.
items.experiment: Evaluate on unseen scenarios and compare with an authored conductor under matched material and compute budgets.

items.title: Contextual bandits for musical action choice
