items.mechanism: Choose among actions using contextual features and feedback while balancing exploration and exploitation.
items.mapping: Select an optional transformation from a small library when explicit, appropriately labelled feedback exists.
items.example: Given section, emotion and energy, choose repeat or answer; observe a later explicit accept/reject label without assuming a full future-state model.
items.controls: Emotion and energy define context; limit exploration during performance; maintain uncertainty when feedback is sparse.
items.failure: Delayed attribution and changing preferences violate simple assumptions. Random exploration can interrupt a phrase.
items.experiment: Compare with fixed action weights and inspect feedback attribution, uncertainty and user control.

items.title: Bar-conditioned symbolic style transfer
items.mechanism: Change declared attributes of existing music while retaining selected content relationships.
items.mapping: Use a theme as content and alter rhythmic intensity or polyphony in future bars, with explicit protected regions.
items.example: Retain lead anchors while requesting a less dense accompaniment; compare decoded activity rather than trusting the requested attribute label.
items.controls: Energy controls validated density attributes; emotion requires an independently calibrated mapping; bar timing defines edit scope.
items.failure: Style, emotion and density are not interchangeable. Transfer can rewrite identity-bearing details.
items.experiment: Check content preservation and control response separately, comparing learned transfer with explicit symbolic edits.

items.title: Pitch-set bitmasks and exhaustive collection spaces
items.mechanism: Represent twelve pitch-class memberships in a twelve-bit integer with an explicit bit convention.
items.mapping: Use complete set membership as a pitch vocabulary, including silent and sparse sets rather than only named scales.
items.example: With bit 0 representing C relative to the root, C-major is mask 2741 and the chromatic collection is 4095. Mask 0 is silence.
items.controls: Emotion chooses authored collection preferences; energy controls rhythm independently; change membership at planned boundaries.
items.failure: A collection is not a cultural practice or a chord progression. Different bit orders can silently change every result.
items.experiment: Round-trip all 4096 masks and compare named anchors with expected pitch classes.

items.title: Transposition/inversion set-class orbits
items.mechanism: Group collections under declared transposition and optional inversion equivalence.
items.mapping: Browse related harmonic materials without confusing a class representative with its particular voiced realization.
items.example: Compute the minimum bitmask across twelve transpositions and their inversions. That numeric representative is not a Forte catalogue number.
items.controls: Emotion selects candidates within and between classes; energy stays separate; harmonic time controls how a representative is realized.
items.failure: Equivalent collections can have different musical functions, roots and spellings. Collapsing them loses important context.
items.experiment: Enumerate class counts with and without inversion, including the empty set as a separately declared case.

items.title: Modal rebasing and collection rotation
items.mechanism: Rebase a selected collection on one of its included pitches while retaining explicit tonic treatment.
items.mapping: Create related pitch vocabularies for contrast or return, preserving degree-aware motif information where possible.
items.example: Rebase C-major on D to obtain offsets [0,2,3,5,7,9,10]. A mode-zero convention can instead preserve an unrooted custom mask unchanged.
items.controls: Emotion biases allowed modes as a profile hypothesis; energy controls arrangement; announce effective harmonic boundaries.
items.failure: Rotation and transposition are different operations. A scale’s interval pattern alone does not reproduce a modal performance practice.
items.experiment: Verify cardinality, membership and rebasing identities, then test motif preservation after mode changes.

items.title: Complementary pitch collections
items.mechanism: Select the pitch classes absent from a collection within a declared universe.
items.mapping: Use a complement as contrast material or a mutually exclusive answering vocabulary, then plan the join back.
items.example: Within twelve classes, complement is mask XOR 4095. A seven-note collection has a five-note complement.
items.controls: Emotion chooses when contrast is appropriate; energy remains independent; time reserves a route back to the theme.
items.failure: The complement can sharply change harmonic meaning. It is not an automatic emotional opposite or consonant partner.
items.experiment: Check double complementation and cardinality sums; audition prepared versus abrupt complement transitions.

items.title: Affine pitch-class transformations
items.mechanism: Map pitch class p to a*p+b modulo twelve, with invertibility depending on the multiplier.
items.mapping: Explore related interval structures through reflection, transposition and coprime multiplication.
items.example: Multipliers 5 and 7 permute all twelve classes; multiplying by 2 can merge classes and reduce cardinality.
items.controls: Emotion selects permitted transforms; energy does not require a multiplier change; apply at a phrase boundary.
items.failure: An invertible mathematical mapping need not preserve tonal function or recognizable melody.
items.experiment: Verify cardinality for coprime multipliers and explicitly test collisions for non-coprime ones.

items.title: Interval-class vectors and cyclic autocorrelation
items.mechanism: Count pitch-pair relationships independently of a particular voicing.
items.mapping: Use interval content as one descriptor when retrieving or contrasting collections, alongside root and functional information.
items.example: C-E-G has interval-class counts [0,0,1,1,1,0]. A tritone contributes one unordered pair, not two.
items.controls: Emotion mapping may hypothesize interval preferences; energy remains rhythmic; section time constrains retrieval and transition.
items.failure: Different collections can share interval content. An interval vector does not measure tension, pleasantness or cultural meaning directly.
items.experiment: Check that vector entries sum to n*(n-1)/2 and compare equal-vector collections without claiming they are identical.

items.title: Pitch-set proximity and mutation graphs
items.mechanism: Connect collections through declared small membership changes or transformation relationships.
items.mapping: Plan harmonic colour paths by adding, removing or moving one pitch class at a time.
items.example: A Hamming-distance-one edge toggles one membership bit; preserve essential theme anchors while searching toward a target set.
items.controls: Emotion selects target vocabularies; energy controls part activity; harmonic time determines when a set change becomes active.
items.failure: Small bit distance is not necessarily small perceptual distance. Changing a tonic-defining pitch can be structurally large.
items.experiment: Compare mathematical distance, common tones and listener judgments of continuity with explicit voicing control.

items.title: Musical torus and lattice walks
items.mechanism: Use a periodic pitch lattice whose coordinates map to pitch classes through an explicit formula.
items.mapping: Move a symbolic cursor through chromatic and fourths-related directions, mapping the path into a melody or harmonic route.
items.example: For p=(x+5*y) mod 12, moving right adds one semitone and moving up adds five. A 12-by-12 torus repeats each pitch class twelve times.
items.controls: Emotion selects path tendencies; energy affects rhythm and accents; time controls path sampling and phrase targets.
items.failure: There are not 144 independent pitch classes. Visual closeness and pitch-class equality encode different relationships.
items.experiment: Check seams, directional steps and repeated labels; compare lattice paths with direct interval sequences.

items.title: Symmetry and limited transposition
items.mechanism: Identify transformations that preserve a collection, producing repeated equivalent images.
items.mapping: Use symmetric collections as stable colour fields or as contrasting material with fewer distinct transpositions.
items.example: The whole-tone set [0,2,4,6,8,10] is invariant under transposition by two semitones and has two distinct transpositions.
items.controls: Emotion chooses a tested colour palette; energy changes realization; section time determines how symmetry is broken or restored.
items.failure: Symmetry can reduce tonal orientation, but does not imply a particular feeling. Different voicings can obscure the same invariance.
items.experiment: Enumerate stabilizing transforms and distinct images, then listen to rooted and unrooted realizations.

items.title: Directional pitch-set quantization
items.mechanism: Map an incoming or proposed pitch to an allowed pitch under nearest, upward, downward or membership-filter rules.
items.mapping: Use quantization as a constrained decoder for stochastic/agent proposals, preserving original release addresses.
items.example: Between C4 and D4, C-sharp4 maps to C4 under nearest-with-downward-tie policy; upward maps to D4. Empty membership suppresses attacks.
items.controls: Emotion selects the vocabulary; energy controls event selection; edits affect future attacks, while active notes keep their recorded targets.
items.failure: Nearest snapping can collapse several source notes onto one pitch and erase ornaments or independent voices.
items.experiment: Test full MIDI boundaries, ties, collisions and releases after a collection edit, then inspect preserved melodic contour.

items.title: Gesture-to-score chronologies
items.mechanism: Separate an ordered score event sequence from the times at which a performer requests its next event.
items.mapping: Let a person control when an authored or generated onset occurs while the composer supplies pitch and phrase context.
items.example: One accepted gesture requests one simultaneous note/chord group; holding the input does not authorize an entire melody.
items.controls: The wheel changes future material; energy changes realization; gesture time and arrangement time remain separate records.
items.failure: Early queues, late recovery and long rests require explicit policies. This is not equivalent to a phrase-launch button.
items.experiment: Use missed-note and late-entry scenarios and ask participants to predict the musical consequence of a gesture.

items.title: Landmark and target synchronization
items.mechanism: Coordinate local musical progress toward declared future positions rather than conflating tempo and position.
items.mapping: Let an answering phrase recover toward a future bar or cadence without bursting through all missed attacks.
items.example: After a delay, choose a reachable next phrase boundary; any duration compression is explicitly bounded and labelled as a heuristic.
items.controls: Emotion changes material, not recovery authority; energy remains separate; time supplies the landmark and confidence.
items.failure: Aggressive correction can destroy phrasing. A local heuristic is not an implementation of Antescofo’s full synchronization algorithms.
items.experiment: Measure phase, tempo and perceived control independently during late input, skipped material and role changes.

items.title: Phase-preserving groove launch
items.mechanism: Start a repeating pattern on a shared phase rather than resetting its cycle to the arrival of the request.
items.mapping: Queue bass or percussion entrances at compatible boundaries while preserving the current arrangement position.
items.example: A request halfway through a bar can enter next bar at phase zero; a legato join needs a separately declared policy.
items.controls: Energy can request layer entrances; emotion changes eligible cells; timing authority decides the effective boundary.
items.failure: Beat alignment is not harmonic validity or identical song position. Queued and sounding states must be distinct.
items.experiment: Check late joins, odd meters and section changes; compare expected versus actual entry boundaries.

items.title: Score-aware human tempo following
items.mechanism: Estimate performed tempo using elapsed score beats associated with observed gestures.
items.mapping: Follow a designated performer or confidence-weighted group while preserving a separate phase-correction policy.
items.example: Two gestures two score beats apart and one second apart imply 120 BPM; they do not imply 60 BPM merely because there were two taps.
items.controls: Emotion and energy may affect intended expression but must not override clock ownership; time estimates carry confidence.
items.failure: Rests, repeated presses and recovery jumps corrupt naive inter-tap estimation. Dense parts should not dominate by event count alone.
items.experiment: Compare fixed clock, designated conductor and bounded group following, measuring drift, oscillation and enjoyment.

items.title: Mixed-initiative musical arrangement
items.mechanism: Distribute proposal, acceptance and execution authority between a person and an automated system.
items.mapping: Allow autonomous bounded development while the person controls targets, locks, recall and rejection.
items.example: The system proposes a counterline; Conduct mode may enter it at a declared phrase boundary, while Suggest mode waits for acceptance.
items.controls: The wheel supplies expressive intention; energy supplies activity; future commitment boundaries make intervention predictable.
items.failure: More automation can obscure the person’s contribution. Explanations must follow actual committed actions rather than invented narratives.
items.experiment: Compare authority modes at equal material budgets and measure perceived control, contribution recognition and musical preference separately.
